unit_label: Module B unit 2: Risks in Banking Business

facts.statement: Banking business lines (as listed in the Basel framework table in the courseware): corporate finance (mergers and acquisitions, underwriting, securitisation, IPOs); trading and sales (fixed income, equity, foreign exchange, commodities, own positions, treasury); retail banking (retail and private banking, card services); commercial banking (project finance, export finance, trade finance, factoring, leasing, lending, guarantees); payments and settlement; agency services (custody, corporate agency, corporate trust); asset management; and retail brokerage. For risk management, exposures are grouped into the banking book, the trading portfolio and off-balance sheet exposures. Operational risk can trigger huge losses, and the key driver in every business line is enhancing risk adjusted expected return.

The banking book includes all advances, deposits and borrowings, usually from commercial and retail banking. Its assets and liabilities are normally held until maturity, accounted on the accrual system (revenue is recognised when earned and expenses when incurred, whatever the timing of cash), not marked to market, and attract capital charge on credit risk, not market risk. Because they are held to maturity, maturity mismatches create liquidity risk; interest rate changes during the period affect net interest margin (interest rate risk); the asset side gives default or credit risk; and operational risk arises from failures of people, systems and processes or external events. The banking book is mainly exposed to liquidity, interest rate, credit and operational risks, and not to market risk since it is not open to the market.

The trading book includes all assets that are marketable. Its positions are not held until maturity but liquidated in the market after a holding period, on a mark-to-market basis with the difference between market price and book value taken to profit and loss. It mostly comprises fixed income securities, equities, foreign exchange holdings and commodities held on the bank's own account, plus derivatives held for trading or hedging them. It is mainly exposed to market risk (including liquidation risk, since instruments with low trading volume may be hard to sell), default or credit risk (including counterparty failure) and operational risk. The courseware says investments Held for Trading are those from which a gain is expected from movement in rates and are to be sold within 90 days.

Under the Reserve Bank's Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio Directions, 2025, a bank classifies its entire investment portfolio (except investments in its subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates) into three categories: Held to Maturity (HTM), Available for Sale (AFS) and Fair Value through Profit and Loss (FVTPL), with Held for Trading (HFT) as a separate sub-category within FVTPL; the category is decided before or at acquisition and documented. A security can be classified under HTM only if it is acquired with the objective of collecting contractual cash flows and its cash flows are solely payments of principal and interest (SPPI). Classification depends on the objective of acquisition and the SPPI criterion, not on whether the security counts for statutory liquidity; similar securities, even from the same lot, can go to different categories if acquired with different objectives.

Off-balance sheet exposures are contingent: guarantees, committed or backup credit lines and letters of credit create payment obligations contingent on an event, and are also called non-fund based exposures or credit facilities; there is no cash outflow when the commitment is issued, but if the customer fails on the due date the bank must meet or fund it. Derivatives such as swaps, futures, forwards, options and foreign currency contracts are off-balance sheet market exposures. A contingent exposure can become fund-based and then belong to the banking book or trading book; off-balance sheet exposures may carry liquidity, interest rate, market, credit and operational risk.

Liquidity risk is the inability to obtain funds to meet cash flow obligations at a reasonable rate; it arises mainly from funding long-term assets with short-term liabilities, which exposes the bank to rollover or refinancing risk. Funding risk is the need to replace net outflows from unanticipated withdrawal or non-renewal of deposits or premature closure of term deposits; time risk is the need to compensate for non-receipt of expected inflows (performing assets becoming non-performing, borrowers not paying instalments on due dates); call risk arises from crystallisation of contingent liabilities when customers do not meet commitments, and from being unable to take up profitable opportunities.

Interest rate risk is the exposure of a bank's revenue to adverse movements in interest rates, affecting net interest income or net interest margin (earnings view) or the market value of equity (economic value view). Gap or mismatch risk arises from holding assets, liabilities and off-balance sheet items with different principal amounts, maturities or repricing dates. Basis risk is the risk that rates on different assets, liabilities and off-balance sheet items move by different amounts (for example a floating rate loan linked to the repo rate funded by a fixed rate deposit). Yield curve risk arises when instruments are priced off different benchmarks or maturities (for example 91-day and 364-day treasury bills) and the yield curve moves non-parallel; it is a form of basis risk. Embedded option risk arises from prepayment of loans, exercise of call or put options on bonds or debentures and premature withdrawal of term deposits when rates change. Reinvestment risk is uncertainty about the rate at which future cash flows can be reinvested. Net interest position risk arises when a bank has more earning assets than paying liabilities, so a fall in rates reduces net interest income and a rise increases it.

Market risk is the risk of adverse deviation of the mark-to-market value of the trading portfolio due to market movements during the holding period, also called price risk; it covers the part of interest rate risk that affects the price of interest rate instruments, pricing risk for equity and commodity positions (banks in India are not permitted to take trading positions in commodities, the courseware says) and foreign currency risk. Forex or exchange risk is the risk of loss from adverse exchange rate movements while a bank has an open position, spot or forward. Market liquidity risk arises when a bank cannot conclude a large transaction in an instrument near the current market price. Credit risk is the potential that a borrower or counterparty fails to meet obligations on agreed terms; counterparty risk is a variant arising from the trading partner's refusal or inability to perform (Herstatt risk, with which the Basel prescription began, the courseware says); country risk is non-performance caused by constraints imposed by a country.

The Basel Committee defines operational risk as the risk of loss resulting from inadequate or failed internal processes, people and systems or from external events. Strategic risk and reputation risk are not covered by that definition. Operational risk includes fraud, communication, documentation, competence, model, cultural, external events, legal, regulatory, compliance and system risk. Transaction risk is the risk from fraud, failed business processes and inability to maintain business continuity and manage information. Compliance risk is the risk of legal or regulatory sanction, financial loss or loss of reputation from failure to comply with laws, regulations, codes of conduct and standards of good practice. Strategic risk is the risk from adverse business decisions, improper implementation or lack of responsiveness to industry changes. Reputational risk is the risk from negative public opinion arising from crystallisation of credit, market or operational risk, so it is normally an indirect risk.

Model risk is the gap between the value predicted by a model and the value actually observed, affecting pricing models (profit and loss) and risk measurement models (risk assessment). It arises from incorrect or non-relevant assumptions, ignoring one or more parameters, errors of statistical technique or insufficient data points, and incorrect judgment on outliers. Models are validated through back testing, carried out by personnel not involved in the design of the model.

payload.title: The business lines of a bank and the three groupings of exposure
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Business line | Typical activities |
| --- | --- |
| **Corporate finance** | **mergers and acquisitions, underwriting, securitisation, IPOs** |
| **Trading and sales** | **fixed income, equity, forex, commodities**, own positions, **treasury** |
| **Retail banking** | retail and **private banking**, **card services** |
| **Commercial banking** | **project, export and trade finance**, **factoring, leasing**, lending, **guarantees** |
| **Payments and settlement** | funds transfer, clearing and settlement |
| **Agency services** | **custody**, corporate agency, **corporate trust** |
| **Asset management** | discretionary and non-discretionary funds |
| **Retail brokerage** | execution and full service |

For risk purposes the exposures fall in **three groups**: the **banking book**, the **trading book** and **off-balance sheet exposures**. Whatever the line, the aim is **higher risk adjusted expected return**, and **operational risk** can cause very large losses.

payload.title: The banking book
payload.core_explanation_md:
Holds **advances, deposits and borrowings**.

**Characteristics**
- **Held to maturity**.
- **Accrual accounting** (revenue recorded **when earned**, expenses **when incurred**, whatever the cash timing).
- **No mark-to-market**.
- Capital charge for **credit risk**, **not market risk**.

**Risks it carries**
| Risk | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **Liquidity** | held to maturity, so **maturity mismatches** leave excess or shortfall of funds |
| **Interest rate** | rates change over the life, hitting **net interest margin** |
| **Credit (default)** | borrowers fail to pay **principal or interest** |
| **Operational** | **people, system, process failures**, external events |

**Not market risk**: the banking book is **not open to the market**.

payload.title: The trading book and how investments are classified today
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Trading book**: **marketable** assets, **sold after a holding period** (not held to maturity), **marked to market** (difference between market price and book value goes to **profit and loss**). Mainly **fixed income, equity, forex and commodity holdings on the bank's own account**, plus **derivatives held for trading or hedging**.

**Risks**: **market risk** (including **liquidation risk** for thinly traded instruments), **credit/default and counterparty risk**, **operational risk**.

**Classification under the Reserve Bank's 2025 Directions** (older books speak of HFT/AFS/HTM with a 90-day rule for HFT; that rule is **not** how the Directions classify today)
- **Three categories**: **HTM, AFS and FVTPL**; **HFT is a sub-category inside FVTPL**.
- The category is **decided before or at acquisition** and **documented**.
- **HTM** only if the **objective is to collect contractual cash flows** and the cash flows are **solely payments of principal and interest (SPPI)**.
- Classification follows **objective and SPPI**, **not** whether the security counts toward **statutory liquidity**; **similar securities from one lot can sit in different categories** if bought for different objectives.

payload.title: Off-balance sheet exposures
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Contingent** commitments: **guarantees, committed or backup credit lines, letters of credit**. Also called **non-fund based exposures**.

- **No cash goes out** when the commitment is issued.
- If the customer **fails on the due date**, the bank **must meet or fund it**; the exposure then becomes **fund based** and falls in the **banking book or trading book**.
- **Derivatives** (swaps, futures, forwards, options, forex contracts) are **off-balance sheet market exposures**.

**Risks**: **liquidity, interest rate, market, credit and operational**.

payload.title: Liquidity risk and its three forms
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Liquidity risk** = **not being able to raise funds at a reasonable rate to meet cash flow obligations**; it comes mainly from **funding long-term assets with short-term liabilities** (**rollover or refinancing risk**).

| Type | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| **Funding risk** | replacing **net outflows** from **unexpected withdrawal, non-renewal or premature closure of deposits** |
| **Time risk** | **expected inflows do not arrive**: performing assets turn **non-performing**, instalments unpaid |
| **Call risk** | **contingent liabilities crystallise** when customers do not meet commitments; also **missing profitable opportunities** for want of funds |

payload.title: The six faces of interest rate risk
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Interest rate risk** = adverse effect of rate moves on **net interest income or margin** (earnings view) or on the **market value of equity** (economic value view).

| Type | In one line | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Gap / mismatch** | **different amounts, maturities or repricing dates** of assets and liabilities | a **2-year fixed rate asset** funded by a **6-month liability** |
| **Basis** | **different rates move by different amounts** | **repo-linked loan** funded by a **fixed rate deposit** |
| **Yield curve** | **different benchmarks or maturities** and a **non-parallel** curve shift; a kind of basis risk | **364-day T-bill asset** funded at the **91-day T-bill** rate |
| **Embedded option** | rate moves trigger **prepayment, call/put exercise, early withdrawal** | borrowers repay when rates fall |
| **Reinvestment** | **uncertain rate** for **reinvesting** future cash flows | a depositor shifts to a bank paying slightly more |
| **Net interest position** | **more earning assets than paying liabilities** | **falling rates cut NII; rising rates raise it** |

payload.title: Market risk and credit risk, with their sub-types
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Market (price) risk**: adverse **mark-to-market** change in the **trading portfolio** during the holding period. It covers: **interest rate price risk**, **equity and commodity price risk**, and **foreign currency risk**.
- **Forex (exchange) risk**: loss from adverse exchange rates while holding an **open position**, **spot or forward**.
- **Market liquidity risk**: cannot trade a **large deal near the current price**.

**Credit risk**: a **borrower or counterparty fails to meet obligations** as agreed; loans and corporate bonds are the largest source.
- **Counterparty risk**: the **trading partner refuses or cannot perform**; usually **transient** and linked to trading.
- **Country risk**: non-performance because of **constraints imposed by a country**, outside the borrower's control.

payload.title: Operational risk and the risks outside its definition
payload.core_explanation_md:
**BCBS definition**: **risk of loss from inadequate or failed internal processes, people and systems, or from external events**.

**Outside the definition**: **strategic risk** and **reputation risk**.

**Within operational risk**: **fraud, communication, documentation, competence, model, cultural, external events, legal, regulatory, compliance and system risk**.

| Risk | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Transaction** | **fraud (internal or external)**, **failed processes**, **inability to keep business going and manage information** |
| **Compliance** | **legal or regulatory sanction, financial or reputation loss** from **not following laws, regulations, codes and good practice** (also called **integrity risk**) |
| **Strategic** | **bad business decisions**, **poor implementation**, **slow response to industry change** |
| **Reputational** | **negative public opinion** after credit, market or operational risk **crystallises**; **an indirect risk** |

payload.title: Model risk
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Model risk** = the **gap between what a model predicts and what is actually observed**. It affects **pricing models** (profit and loss) and **risk measurement models** (risk assessment).

**Causes**: **wrong or outdated assumptions**; **ignoring a parameter** for simplicity; **statistical errors or too few data points**; **wrong judgment on outliers**.

**Control**: **back testing**, done by people **not involved in designing** the model.

payload.title: Basis risk on a floating rate loan funded by a fixed rate deposit
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: a bank accepts a two-year deposit at a fixed 7.00% and lends the money as a two-year loan priced at the repo rate plus 3.00%, with the repo rate at 6.50%. Find the margin now and after the repo rate falls by 0.35 percentage points, and after it rises by 0.35.

worked_steps.description: Margin after a 0.35 fall in repo.
Margin after a 0.35 rise in repo.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: The margin is 2.50% now, 2.15% after a fall and 2.85% after a rise: the fixed deposit rate does not move with the repo rate

self_check.prompt_text: What would happen to the margin if the deposit were also floating and linked to the repo rate?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Both sides would move together and the margin would be much steadier, so basis risk falls.

payload.title: Repricing gap and the effect of a rate move on net interest income
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: in the one-year bucket a bank has rate sensitive assets of ₹900 crore and rate sensitive liabilities of ₹650 crore. Estimate the effect on net interest income over the year if interest rates rise by 1 percentage point and, separately, if they fall by 1 percentage point, assuming all items reprice at the start of the year.
payload.final_answer_with_unit: Net interest income rises by about ₹2.5 crore if rates rise 1 point and falls by about ₹2.5 crore if they fall 1 point

self_check.prompt_text: Which direction of rates hurts a bank with a negative gap?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A rise in rates hurts it, because more liabilities than assets reprice upward.

payload.stem_md: A bank accepts a fixed 6.75% deposit and lends at the repo rate plus 3.25%. The repo rate is 6.00% and then falls to 5.50%. What is the margin on the loan after the fall, in per cent?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 2 decimal places.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Loan rate after the fall = 5.50 + 3.25 = 8.75%. Margin = 8.75 − 6.75 = 2.00%.

payload.stem_md: In the one-year bucket a bank has rate sensitive assets of ₹1,240 crore and rate sensitive liabilities of ₹1,515 crore. By how many crore rupees does net interest income change over the year if rates rise by 0.5 percentage point and everything reprices at the start (give a negative number as a positive amount of reduction)?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 3 decimal places.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Gap = 1,240 − 1,515 = −275. Effect = −275 × 0.5% = −1.375, so net interest income falls by ₹1.375 crore.
